q: Five factors in the competitive-vs-sole-source call.
a: Data rights sufficiency · switching/qualification costs · industrial base capability · honest urgency · second-source economics.

q: What inventory precedes a sustainment competition decision?
a: Data rights, deliverables (source/build/interfaces), GFP/tooling, licenses, funding.

q: What can never justify a bridge?
a: Lack of advance planning.

q: What factors drive competitive vs. sole-source for the follow-on?
a: Data rights and technical data sufficiency · qualification/switching costs and time · industrial base capability · urgency honestly assessed · lifecycle economics of a second source. Facts on each, in the file.

q: How do you find out if other sources can perform?
a: Fresh sources-sought and RFIs · industry days · capability analysis against the tech data package · other services'/agencies' experience with similar builds.

q: And if truly no one else can?
a: RFO 6.103-1, one responsible source — with the J&A at the right approval tier and market research that would survive a competitor's lawyer reading it.

q: Three types of authority — which one binds nothing?
a: Express, implied, apparent — apparent binds nothing.

q: All six ratification elements.
a: Proper-if-CO · benefit · ratifier's actual authority · fair & reasonable price · funds then and now · Legal.

q: Who ratifies a $500K unauthorized commitment? A $90K one?
a: $500K → HCA (delegable); $90K → COCO.

q: Five elements of a valid contract.
a: Offer/acceptance · consideration · competency · legality · certainty of terms.

q: What if the Government received no benefit?
a: Then it can't be ratified — a ratification requires acceptance or benefit. The contractor's remedy shifts to a claim (or quantum meruit through Legal); my job is the documented record either way.

q: The person who did it refuses to write a statement.
a: Document the refusal, reconstruct the facts from correspondence and witnesses, and proceed — the package needs the story, and the refusal itself goes in the record.

q: Is implied authority real authority?
a: Yes — authority reasonably inferred from a position's duties is legally valid. Apparent authority is the trap: looking authorized isn't being authorized.

q: Two categories of protected information under RFO 3.104.
a: Source selection information; contractor bid/proposal data.

q: Your first two containment actions on a bad disclosure.
a: Legal immediately; identify/contain — recipient deletes with signed confirmation.

q: Where does the decision go if the disclosure impacts the procurement?
a: The HCA.

q: Name three prevention practices you'd brief a new source selection team.
a: Two-person review before release · encryption with separate passwords · disable auto-complete · SSI cover sheets (any three).

q: The recipient says she deleted it — done?
a: Not on her word: signed affidavit confirming deletion of all copies, and the determination still has to be written. The record closes it, not the reply email.

q: What if it went to an actual offeror?
a: That's the high-impact branch: presumptive taint of the competition. HCA decision territory — disqualification or cancellation are on the table, with Legal driving.

q: A contractor employee asks your evaluator how the ratings look — violation?
a: Attempting to obtain source selection information is itself a PIA problem. Document it, report it, brief the team — silence is how small probes become disclosures.

q: The three OCI types — and which is hardest to mitigate?
a: Biased ground rules (hardest) · unequal access · impaired objectivity.

q: The three handling tools, in order of preference.
a: Avoid · neutralize · mitigate.

q: Who approves an OCI waiver, and is it delegable?
a: HCA; non-delegable.

q: True or false: unequal access requires showing the contractor acted on the information.
a: False — the access imbalance itself is the conflict.

q: Which type is hardest to mitigate and why?
a: Biased ground rules — once the requirement itself is shaped, a firewall can't un-shape it. Exclusion is the usual outcome.

q: The contractor firewall says the proposal team never saw anything. Enough?
a: A firewall can address unequal access going forward — it does nothing for ground rules already written. Type drives remedy.

q: Who has final say on the mitigation plan?
a: The PCO. Panels and reviewers advise; the decision and the accountability are mine.

q: Recite the seven responsibility standards.
a: Finances · schedule · performance · integrity · organization/experience/controls · equipment/facilities · qualified & eligible.

q: Which two system checks precede award, and at what threshold does the second apply?
a: SAM exclusions always; FAPIIS over SAT ($350K).

q: What happens when a small business is found non-responsible?
a: Referral to SBA — a CoC conclusively establishes responsibility.

q: Doubt about capability cuts in whose favor?
a: The Government's — doubt means no.

q: SBA issues the CoC but you still think they'll fail. Now what?
a: A CoC is conclusive as to responsibility — I award, then protect the Government with administration: a solid QASP, milestone surveillance, and early engagement at the first sign of trouble. (Appeal paths exist in a dollar band — worked with Legal and SBA, not solo.)

q: Can you use responsibility to screen out a contractor you distrust?
a: Only on the standards, only on facts. Distrust without documentation is how a defensible "no" becomes a sustained protest.

q: What's the difference between non-responsible and ineligible?
a: Ineligible = excluded (SAM/debarment) — no award, period. Non-responsible = fails the standards for this award, on today's facts.

q: Four questions market research must answer.
a: Capable sources · commercial or not · small business capability · industry practices (also: bundling justified?).

q: How long is research treated as current?
a: 18 months.

q: Name five research methods.
a: Sources sought · RFI · industry day · SME/vendor engagement · prior-buy history · catalogs (any five).

q: What document downstream decisions cite — and what happens if it was never written?
a: The market research report; undocumented research can't support the J&A/set-aside/CID that relies on it.

q: Your sources-sought got one response. Sole source it?
a: One response to one notice isn't market absence — it's a data point. Widen the net (direct outreach, industry channels, adjacent NAICS) before concluding only one source exists; the J&A will be judged on the effort.

q: How is market research different from a competition requirement?
a: Research is the evidence; competition is the decision. Research tells me whether the Rule of Two is met, whether full-and-open is realistic, whether commercial procedures fit — it doesn't replace any of them.

q: The PM wrote the spec around Vendor X's product. Fix it with research?
a: Backwards — research should shape the requirement, not justify it after the fact. I'd push for a performance-based restatement and use the research to show what the market can actually deliver.

q: The supplies priority order, top to bottom.
a: Inventory → excess → UNICOR → AbilityOne → wholesale → mandatory FSS → commercial.

q: What leads the services ladder?
a: AbilityOne.

q: On an FSS order, who determines the order price fair and reasonable?
a: The ordering contracting officer — GSA's schedule pricing doesn't substitute.

q: The AbilityOne item is pricier than the commercial one. Buy commercial?
a: Mandatory means mandatory — if the item is on the procurement list and meets the need, price alone doesn't unlock the open market. Work fit/availability issues through the program, on the record.

q: Why isn't a schedule buy automatically fair and reasonable?
a: Because GSA negotiated a ceiling across the government, not my quantity, configuration, or competitive moment. Comparing quotes among holders and asking for discounts is the ordering CO's job.

q: The commercial definition in one sentence, including the mod rule.
a: Sold/leased/licensed to the general public (or evolved and available in time), including minor mods that don't alter form, fit, or function.

q: CID: at what threshold is it written, and who approves it?
a: Over SAT ($350K); one level above the CO.

q: Streamlined commercial procedures — cite and ceiling?
Name two things Part 12 gives you and two things it takes away.
a: Gets: no certified data, streamlined terms/FFP preference. Takes: only customary market data rights; Part 49 termination machinery.

q: How do you price it fair and reasonable without cost data?
a: Market evidence: competition first, then catalog/published prices, sales history to other customers, parametric comparisons — and I can require data other than certified where the market evidence is thin.

q: The mod adds an encrypted military datalink. Still minor?
a: Test it against form, fit, and function of the base item — a modification that changes what the item fundamentally is or does takes you out of "minor." That's a facts-and-engineering call, documented in the CID.

q: Termination for cause vs. T4D?
a: Commercial contracts use the commercial clause's cause/convenience framework — Part 49's default machinery (cure notices per 49.x, excess reprocurement) doesn't apply as such. Chain warning: boards love this seam.

q: The three SAP lanes and their dollar boundaries.
a: GPC ≤$15K · POs $15K–$350K · BPAs for repetitive needs.

q: Who is the MPT-to-SAT band reserved for?
a: Small business, unless capable small sources can't be found.

q: What documentation does an under-SAT sole source need?
a: A documented single-source rationale + price reasonableness — no formal J&A.

q: Commercial streamlined ceiling and cite?
Why not spread the tool-crib buy across three GPC swipes?
a: That's splitting a known requirement to evade the MPT — a bright-line violation. One $210K requirement is one purchase-order action with small business first.

q: BPA vs. IDIQ — when does the small path stop fitting?
a: A BPA is an account, not a contract — no obligation until a call. When needs get big, defined, and multi-year, the structure (and the money) belongs in a real vehicle.

q: One quote came back on your $80K buy — award?
a: I can, if I can call the price fair and reasonable — compare to history, catalogs, IGCE, and document it. Reasonableness rides on evidence, not on the count of quotes.

q: State the Rule of Two precisely.
a: Reasonable expectation of two or more capable small businesses submitting offers at fair market prices → set aside.

q: Sole-source ceilings: HUBZone other? SDVOSB other? 8(a) DoD?
What form documents specialist coordination?
a: DD Form 2579.

q: Subcontracting plan thresholds?
a: $900K; $2M construction.

q: Only one small business responds to your set-aside — now what?
a: If the offer is fair-market priced, award — the Rule of Two tests the expectation, not the final count. Document what changed between research and offers.

q: The requirement's been in the 8(a) program — can you compete it full-and-open now?
a: Not unilaterally: once in 8(a), it stays unless SBA agrees to release it. That's the follow-on trap on 8(a) requirements.

q: When does 8(a) sole source need a J&A?
a: DoD: not below $100M. The program's statutory basis covers it — that's the 'authorized by statute' lane.

q: Recite the four SAMO carve-outs.
a: SAP · statute · in-scope mods · orders under existing vehicles.

q: Name all seven RFO 6.103 exceptions, in any order.
a: One source · urgency · industrial mobilization/R&D · international agreement · statute · national security · public interest.

q: Your J&A is $18M — who approves? $95M (DoD)? $160M (DoD)?
a: $18M → Competition Advocate; $95M DoD → HPA/PEO (DoD line is $150M); $160M DoD → SPE.

q: How long do you have to post a J&A to SAM.gov after award? After an urgency award?
a: 14 days; 30 days for urgency.

q: Only one offer came in on your competitive solicitation — now what?
a: If the solicitation allowed under 30 days for offers, consult the requiring activity and resolicit for at least 30. If interest was real but only one firm bid, find out why — get feedback, document it, and use it to open the next competition. The award can still be made if the price is fair and reasonable.

q: What's the difference between full-and-open after exclusion of sources and other than full-and-open?
a: Exclusion still competes — among a deliberately narrowed field (a set-aside is the everyday example). "Other than" means one or very few sources under an RFO 6.103 exception.

q: Who approves your $40M J&A? …and a $15M one?
a: $40M → HPA/PEO. $15M → Competition Advocate. (Know your ladder cold — boards love the second ask.)

q: The program wants a bridge while the follow-on catches up. Fine?
a: Only for a genuinely unforeseen cause — a protest, a directed strategy change, a regulatory change. "We didn't plan" is never a valid basis, and repeat bridges escalate to higher approval each time.

q: The three exchange types and the line between them.
a: Clarifications (minor, no revisions) · communications (pre-range) · discussions (post-range, meaningful, all in range).

q: Who evaluates, who decides, who runs the business side?
a: SSEB · SSA · PCO.

q: When can you award without discussions?
a: Solicitation said so and initial proposals support it.

q: What must a post-award debrief include — and exclude?
a: Include: evaluated result, significant weaknesses, ranking/rationale. Exclude: other offerors' proposal contents.

q: Award without discussions — when is that OK?
a: If the solicitation preserved it and the initial proposals support a clean award. On large, complex actions, discussions usually earn their keep — say you'd weigh it, not autopilot it.

q: An evaluator wants to ping an offeror about an ambiguity before the range.
a: That's a communication — through me, documented, no proposal revisions. The moment it invites a revision, it's discussions, and discussions have rules.

q: Can price be a rating like technical?
a: No — cost/price is evaluated (analysis, realism where applicable) but never adjectivally rated. It competes in the tradeoff as a number with analysis behind it.

q: What makes discussions 'meaningful'?
a: Each offeror hears its own significant weaknesses and deficiencies with enough substance to respond — tailored, not generic, and even-handed across the range.

topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
q: Current certified-data threshold, and the date line that changed it?
a: $10M for actions entered after 30 Jun 2026 (FY26 NDAA §1804); $2.5M for earlier contracts and their mods.

topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
q: Recite CLAWM — and where do the exceptions live in the RFO?
a: Commercial · Law/regulation · Adequate price competition · Waiver (HCA) · commercial Mods — RFO 15.403-2.

topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
q: Which analysis is always required? When does cost realism apply?
a: Price analysis, always (15.404-1); cost realism on competitive cost-type source selections (15.404-3).

topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
q: All five elements of defective pricing.
a: Was cost/pricing data · existed pre-agreement · not disclosed · relied upon · increased the price.

topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
q: CPFF fee ceilings for R&D, most others, A&E.

topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
q: What's the difference between certified and other-than-certified cost or pricing data?
a: The data can be identical — the certificate is the difference. Other-than-certified is what you request to determine price reasonableness when an exception applies; no certificate, no defective-pricing remedy.

topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
q: The contractor did a 'sweep' after agreement and found new data — now what?
a: Sweeps are recommended, not required. Before award: incorporate — if the corrected price is lower, adjust down; if higher, the contractor generally eats it unless it's unreasonable, and you may reopen. After award: that's defective pricing — the Government is entitled to a price reduction plus interest; bring in Legal.

topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
q: The contractor refuses to provide further support during fact-finding.
a: Document exactly what was requested and refused, use DCMA/DCAA to press the field organization, elevate through the contractor's management — and remember I can't award without determining the price fair and reasonable. No data, no deal, and the file shows why.

topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
q: When would you get DCAA vs. DCMA support?
a: Field pricing support scales with dollars and type — DCMA forward-pricing rate support around $2.5M+ (fixed-price) / $10M+ (cost-type); DCAA audit at $10M+ (fixed-price) / $100M+ (cost-type). Below those, my pricing office and I work it.

q: Five type-selection factors.
a: Requirement definition · estimate confidence · technical risk · competition · accounting system · acquisition history (any five).

q: The PTA formula.
a: PTA = (Ceiling − Target Price) ÷ Gov share + Target Cost.

q: Two gates every cost-type contract must clear.
a: Adequate accounting system; D&F.

q: E.O. 14402 justification thresholds — DoD and most agencies.
a: DoD $100M; most agencies $10M.

q: Walk me through the PTA.
a: The point where the ceiling takes over: (ceiling price minus target price) divided by the Government's share, plus target cost. Past it, each cost dollar comes out of profit — the contractor is effectively on FFP from there to the ceiling.

q: Why not FFP the development effort — doesn't it protect us?
a: A contractor forced to price the unknowable pads the price or fails trying — both cost the Government more. FFP on high-uncertainty work is risk denial, not risk transfer.

q: CPFF vs. CPIF in one sentence each?
a: CPFF: fee fixed at award regardless of cost outcome — buys effort under uncertainty. CPIF: fee slides with cost performance inside a min/max — buys cost discipline when a credible target exists.

q: All six fair-opportunity exceptions.
a: Urgency · only-one-capable · logical follow-on · minimum guarantee · statute · order-level small business set-aside.

q: Order-debrief breakpoint? GAO order-protest thresholds?
a: $7.5M; $35M DoD / $10M civilian (or scope/period/ceiling growth at any value).

q: What document supports an over-SAT exception, and who approves at $12M?
a: A D&A; $12M → Competition Advocate.

q: What makes a follow-on 'logical' enough to use the exception?
a: Genuine continuity economics — the original order was competed (or properly excepted), and switching performers mid-stream would cost duplication the Government can't recover. Used sparingly, documented hard, and it weakens every time you stack it.

q: A holder complains the last three orders all went to one firm.
a: They get the ombudsman, and I get a look in the mirror: consideration has to be real — rotating "considered but lost" paperwork isn't fair opportunity.

q: Can you set aside an order for small business on a mixed vehicle?
a: Yes — order-level set-asides are a recognized exception lane; document the Rule-of-Two logic among holders.

q: The exercise gates, all of them.
a: Funds · existing need · most advantageous (fresh market/price look) · not excluded in SAM · performance considered.

q: What happens legally if the notice date passes?
a: The unilateral right lapses — continuation is bilateral.

q: The services duration rail and the extension-clause cap.
a: ~5 years base+options; 6-month extension cap.

q: Three situations where you shouldn't use options at all.
a: No realistic exercise chance · volatile pricing · full requirement already known and funded.

q: Market prices dropped 15% since award. Exercise anyway?
a: Only if I can still call the option price the most advantageous path after an informal market check — otherwise the honest answer may be a new competition. The option price was reasonable then; the gate asks about now.

q: You missed the notice window by a week.
a: The unilateral right is gone. If continuing is still best, it's a bilateral agreement — negotiated, documented, and the contractor holds leverage. Then I fix the suspense system that let it slip.

q: Performance is shaky — exercise and 'manage it'?
a: The performance gate exists for exactly this. Options are leverage: a contractor renewed despite flags learns the flags don't matter. Decide with the record, not with inertia.

q: Direct vs. assisted — the one-sentence difference and the document assisted requires.
a: Direct: our CO orders on their vehicle; assisted: their shop buys for us — signed interagency agreement required.

q: When does the Economy Act apply, and what paperwork rides with it?
a: Only absent a more specific authority; MIPR + D&F (Government's interest, not better from private sector).

q: Does sending funds to another agency stop the fiscal clock?
a: No — purpose, time, and amount rules travel with the money.

q: Why not just MIPR it and let them worry about it?
a: Because accountability doesn't transfer with the money — the requirement, the fiscal rules, and the outcome are still ours. The D&F exists to prove we chose this lane deliberately.

q: Direct vs. assisted — who's the contracting officer?
a: Direct: our CO places the order under their contract's terms. Assisted: their CO acts for us under the interagency agreement — which is why that agreement must define roles before a dollar moves.

q: When is the Economy Act the wrong cite?
a: Whenever a more specific authority exists — schedules and GWACs carry their own authority. Citing the Economy Act for a schedule order tells the board you memorized a name, not a framework.

q: TPA — say what each letter tests.
a: Time = availability + bona fide need; Purpose = appropriated use; Amount = ADA limits.

q: Colors and clocks: O&M, RDT&E, procurement.
a: 1 · 2 · 3 years.

q: Severable vs. non-severable funding rules.
a: Severable ≤12 months, may cross FYs, current funds; non-severable fully funded up front.

q: LoC vs. LoF — which contract, what notice?
a: LoC on fully funded cost contracts, LoF on incremental — ~75% notice.

q: The financing order of preference.
a: Private → customary (PBP preferred) → unusual → advance payments.

q: The contractor blew past the ceiling without notice and wants more money.
a: The limitation clause allocates that risk: no timely notice, no entitlement to overrun funding — the Government may fund, but doesn't have to. Facts first: when did they know, when did they tell.

q: Why are performance-based payments preferred over progress payments?
a: They pay for demonstrated events, not incurred cost — better incentive alignment, recoverable in default, and less administration on costs.

q: Can expired funds pay a claim on an old contract?
a: Yes — within their 5-year expired window, for adjustments to obligations properly made when current. After cancellation, no.

q: The three funding scenarios and the rights each produces.
a: All Government $ → unlimited; mixed → GPR (converting to unlimited after the period); all private $ → limited (tech data)/restricted (software).

q: Who bears the burden of proving a restriction?
a: The contractor.

q: What may the Government do with GPR data?
a: Any Government purpose — including competitive reprocurement under protections; no commercial use.

q: The challenge sequence, and what you must not do while it runs.
a: Written challenge → contractor response (60 days) → CO final decision → appeal; honor the markings until resolved.

q: Deliverables arrived unmarked. What rights do we have?
a: Unmarked data delivered under the clause is effectively unrestricted in the Government's hands — but confirm through Legal before acting on it; the honest move is verifying, not pouncing.

q: Can GPR data go to a competitor for the sustainment RFP?
a: Yes — Government purposes include competitive reprocurement, with recipients under nondisclosure protections. That's exactly what GPR is for.

q: The contractor says the whole system is proprietary because it 'integrates' their private-expense modules.
a: Integration doesn't launder rights — map component by component. Mixed funding at the component level yields component-level rights, and the assertion list has to be that granular.

q: The four scope-test corners.
a: Competition anticipation · contract type · period · cumulative cost.

q: Unilateral vs. bilateral — which actions belong to each?
a: Unilateral: admin, in-scope change orders, option exercise; bilateral: substantive negotiated changes.

q: Define constructive change and cardinal change in one sentence each.
a: Constructive: Government conduct changes work without formal direction; cardinal: change so profound it exceeds what was competed — potential breach.

q: Against what baseline is mod 100 judged?
a: The original contract, all mods cumulative.

q: Who decides if it's in scope?
a: The PCO, with Legal — documented. It's a judgment call with a test, not a vibe: anticipation, type, period, cumulative cost.

q: A competitor found out about a big unpublicized mod and complained. Your answer?
a: If my scope analysis is in the file and honest, I walk them (and my boss) through it. If the analysis was never done — that's the finding. Publicity follows scope: in-scope mods aren't competed or synopsized; new work is.

q: PM directed extra testing verbally; contractor performed. What is that?
a: A constructive change candidate — Government conduct changed the work. Contractor asserts its costs; I sort entitlement and get the direction channel fixed (all direction through the PCO).

q: The default rule and the four-part exception test.
a: Contractor furnishes; GFP only if best interest · benefit > burden · no substantial risk increase · not otherwise met — all four.

q: Who writes the GFP justification?
a: The requiring activity (PM), to the PCO.

q: Name three clause functions that ride with the property clause.
a: Marking/IUID · loss reporting · property-system administration · disposal (any three).

q: Consequence of delivering GFP late or faulty?
a: Government-caused delay — schedule/equitable-adjustment exposure.

q: Contractor reports a Government-furnished test set stolen.
a: The loss-reporting clause machinery runs: report, investigate, determine liability under the risk allocation, and adjust the property record — with the property administrator carrying the process.

q: Why not furnish property freely if it lowers proposed prices?
a: Because price isn't the only ledger: administration, risk shift, and Government performance obligations all cost. The four-part test is that ledger.

q: When is no justification needed?
a: Property furnished for repair/modification/overhaul work — the property is the requirement there.

q: The obligation caps, before and after the qualifying proposal.
a: 50% of NTE before; 75% after.

q: The definitization clock and its other trigger.
a: 180 days from qualifying proposal; also when obligations reach the caps.

q: Two reasons that never justify a UCA.
a: Lack of planning; administrative convenience.

q: UCO vs. UCA in one sentence.
a: UCO = unpriced unilateral change within an existing contract's scope; UCA = new undefinitized contract action.

q: The contractor is slow-rolling the qualifying proposal. Why might that be?
a: Every month undefinitized is a month of cost-reimbursement-like comfort at negotiation leverage. My tools: the obligation caps bite, progress-payment posture tightens, and the definitization schedule is a contract term — enforce it.

q: Why does fee usually come down at definitization?
a: Weighted guidelines price risk. With actuals on the books, the cost risk the fee would have paid for has partly evaporated — fee follows the remaining risk, not the original unknowns.

q: Do UCAs need clearance? A J&A?
a: Clearance at definitization (award-stage clearance isn't the gate). And the circumstances driving a UCA usually drive a Part 6 exception too — urgency or one-source — so the J&A rides in parallel.

q: Business vs. contract clearance — what each approves.
a: Business = release the solicitation / open negotiations; contract = the award/negotiated result.

q: Why must the reviewer be independent?
a: The selector can't approve the selection — independent senior review before commitment.

q: When does a UCA clear?
a: At definitization.

q: Why two clearances instead of one?
a: Because a sound strategy can still yield a bad deal, and a good deal can implement an unapproved strategy — the gates catch different failures.

q: What does the clearance authority actually check?
a: That the action implements the approved strategy · the price/result is fair and reasonable and supported · the file complies — statute, regulation, policy — before the Government commits.

q: Clearance said no. Now?
a: Fix what they flagged — position, support, or strategy — and return. Clearance friction is cheaper than any failure it prevents; treat the authority as a teammate with veto power.

q: The post-award stay rule, precisely.
a: Stay if filed within 10 days of award or 5 days of the required debrief, whichever is later.

q: Three venues and one distinguishing feature each.
a: Agency — fastest/self-correcting; GAO — 100-day, automatic stay; COFC — binding, injunction instead of stay.

q: Who authorizes an override, and on what two bases?
a: HCA, written: urgent & compelling circumstances, or best interests of the United States.

q: Task-order protest thresholds.
a: $35M DoD / $10M civilian, or scope/period/ceiling growth at any value.

q: Protest filed on day 9 after award, but the debrief was never requested. Stay?
a: Day 9 is inside the 10-day award window — stay applies. The 5-day debrief branch only substitutes when a required debrief was requested and given later.

q: GAO recommendations are 'advisory' — so ignore one?
a: Legally advisory, practically followed — non-compliance is reported to Congress and torches agency credibility. Treat a sustain as a to-do list with a deadline.

q: How do you protest-proof a source selection?
a: You don't — you record-proof it: criteria stated and followed, evaluations contemporaneous and even-handed, meaningful discussions, an SSDD with real comparative reasoning, and a debrief that answers questions instead of provoking them.

q: Four differences between an REA and a claim.
a: Interest (claim only) · decision deadlines (claim) · prep costs (allowable REA / unallowable claim) · formality-certification.

q: Claim certification threshold and the accrual limit.
a: $100K; 6 years from accrual.

q: What is a deemed denial, and what does it start?
a: CO silence past the decision deadline operates as denial — the appeal clock starts.

q: The two appeal routes and their clocks.
a: Board of Contract Appeals, 90 days; COFC, 12 months.

q: The contractor titled it 'REA' but demands a sum certain, certified, 'decision requested.'
a: Substance over label — that's functionally a claim, and the CDA machinery (interest, deadlines) may already be running. Classify with Legal, fast.

q: Why would a contractor choose the REA lane at all?
a: Relationship preservation, allowable prep costs, speed, and settlement flexibility — the claim lane is leverage, but it burns goodwill and time.

q: What must a differing-site-conditions recovery show first?
a: Notice — the clause requires prompt written notice before conditions are disturbed, so the Government can investigate. No notice, weakened recovery.

q: T4C settlement contents — and the profit rule.
a: Costs incurred + reasonable profit on work performed + settlement expenses; no anticipatory profit.

q: The T4D runway, in order.
a: Cure notice → show cause → excusability analysis → T4D notice as final decision.

q: Three classic excusable causes.
a: Acts of God · sovereign/Government acts · fires/epidemics/similar events beyond control without fault.

q: What happens to a T4D later found wrongful?
a: Converts to a T4C — settlement owed instead of costs recovered.

q: What does the contractor get in a T4C settlement?
a: Costs incurred on the terminated work, reasonable profit on what was done, and settlement expenses — not the profit they hoped to earn on work never performed.

q: You defaulted them; the board later finds the failure excusable. Now?
a: The T4D converts to a T4C — with the Government paying settlement instead of collecting reprocurement costs. That's why the excusability record precedes the notice.

q: When would you skip the cure notice?
a: A pure failure to deliver on time — the schedule was the cure period. But when facts are mixed, send it; a needless cure notice costs ten days, a missing one can cost the termination.

q: What makes BAA evaluation lawful competition?
a: Public announcement + stated criteria + independent scientific merit review — selection against the standard, not between offerors.

q: The three SBIR phases and Phase III's special property.
a: I feasibility · II prototype · III production — no cap, sole-source eligible off competed early phases, SBIR rights persist.

q: Two honest reasons to choose an OT — and one dishonest one.
a: Honest: nontraditional participation; terms flexibility a prototype genuinely needs. Dishonest: "skipping the rules.".

q: How is funding one BAA proposal 'competition' without comparing proposals?
a: The BAA is a recognized competitive procedure: broad public announcement, stated criteria, independent merit review. The market competed by proposing; selection is merit against the standard, not against each other.

q: Phase III SBIR sole source — really no J&A?
a: The statutory program carries it when the work derives from competed Phase I/II — that's the authorized-by- statute lane. Document the derivation.

q: When would you steer away from an OT?
a: Traditional performers, well-understood requirements, or when the flexibilities aren't actually needed — OTs trade a mature protections framework for agility; spend that trade only when it buys something.

q: The two Miller-Act-style bonds and whom each protects.
a: Performance bond — the Government's work; payment bond — subs/suppliers who can't lien Government property.

q: The differing-site-conditions notice rule and its reason.
a: Written notice before disturbing the condition, so the Government can investigate.

q: The personal-services test in one sentence.
a: Continuous Government supervision of contractor employees creates an employer-employee relationship — unlawful absent specific authority.

q: PBA's required elements.
a: PWS (or SOO) · measurable standards · QASP · incentives where appropriate.

q: Why can't you pick the A&E firm on price like everything else?
a: Statutory design: qualifications-based selection, then negotiate a fair price with the most qualified — design quality drives lifecycle cost far more than design fee does.

q: What's the difference between a PWS and a SOO?
a: PWS: the Government defines outcomes and standards. SOO: the Government states objectives and offerors propose their own PWS — competition on approach, with the winning PWS becoming the yardstick.

q: The COR is assigning daily tasks to contractor staff 'for efficiency.'
a: That's the personal-services drift in action — direction flows to the contractor's manager against PWS outcomes. Fix the practice, retrain the COR, and check whether the PWS invites it.
